questions.q: A 2-month-old male infant with X-linked recessive Menkes disease develops severe neurologic symptoms due to deficiency of multiple copper-dependent enzymes. Which of the following enzyme deficiencies is responsible for the characteristic poor wound healing, vascular tortuosity, and bone fragility resembling scurvy in this patient?
opts: Tyrosinase deficiency
Cytochrome c oxidase deficiency
Lysyl oxidase deficiency
Ascorbic acid oxidase deficiency
questions.exp: Lysyl oxidase is a copper-dependent enzyme critical for collagen and elastin cross-linking in connective tissue and blood vessels. Its deficiency in Menkes disease results in defective collagen synthesis, leading to poor wound healing, vascular fragility with tortuous and elongated arteries, bone fragility with fractures, and a clinical picture mimicking scurvy. Cytochrome c oxidase causes gray matter neurodegeneration; tyrosinase causes hypopigmentation and abnormal hair color.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: LYSYL OXIDASE is a CROSS-LINKER KNIGHT guarding the COLLAGEN CASTLE WALLS—without copper, he cannot work, so the WALLS CRUMBLE (poor healing), BLOOD VESSEL TOWERS twist and break, and BONE BRIDGES fracture like SCURVY's siege damage.

questions.q: A 19-year-old college student presents with fever, exudative pharyngitis, and tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. On examination, you note petechiae at the junction of hard and soft palate and bilateral periorbital puffiness. Which mechanism best explains the periorbital oedema (Hoagland's sign) in this patient's infectious mononucleosis?
opts: Direct viral invasion of periorbital tissues causing local inflammation
Lymphatic obstruction from profound cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy
Immune complex vasculitis affecting periorbital blood vessels
Increased vascular permeability from circulating EBV-infected B lymphocytes
questions.exp: Hoagland's sign refers to periorbital oedema occurring in ~50% of IM cases during the first week. The mechanism is lymphatic obstruction secondary to profound lymphadenopathy rather than direct viral infection of periorbital tissues. This characteristic sign is highly suggestive of infectious mononucleosis when present.
questions.source: EBV Cutaneous Manifestations (Infectious Mononucleosis, Ampicillin Rash, Gianotti-Crosti)
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Picture a SWOLLEN-EYED KING sitting on a throne surrounded by GIANT NECK PILLOWS (lymph nodes) blocking his face's drainage pipes—his eyes puff up because the lymph superhighway is jammed.

questions.q: A 16-year-old girl develops rubella infection with the characteristic exanthem and enanthem. Which intraoral finding is pathognomonic for rubella and typically appears just before the cutaneous rash?
opts: White spots with reddish halos on the buccal mucosa (Koplik spots)
Rose-pink pinpoint macules or petechiae on the soft palate and uvula (Forchheimer spots)
Small vesicles scattered throughout the oral mucosa
Gray pseudomembranes covering the posterior pharynx
questions.exp: Forchheimer spots are the characteristic enanthem of rubella, consisting of rose-pink pinpoint macules or petechiae on the soft palate and uvula. They appear just prior to or alongside the cutaneous exanthem and are considered pathognomonic for rubella infection. This distinguishes rubella from measles (which presents with Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa).
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Walk into the castle's SOFT PALATE THRONE ROOM where FORCHHEIMER, a rose-colored courtier, sprinkles PINK PETALS on the UVULA CHANDELIER—appearing right BEFORE the main ball (cutaneous rash) begins.

questions.q: A 3-week-old male infant is noted to have large, dark-brown, tightly adherent polygonal scales predominantly over his neck, preauricular region, and lateral face, creating a 'dirty neck' appearance. His mother reports difficult labor delivery. Which of the following distinguishes this condition from ichthyosis vulgaris?
opts: Affected males have sparing of palms and soles; scales encroach upon flexures
Affected individuals present with diminished stratum granulosum on histology
Inheritance pattern is autosomal dominant with semi-dominance
Symptoms classically improve during warm, humid summer months
questions.exp: Recessive X-linked ichthyosis (RXLI) is caused by steroid sulfatase deficiency, leading to cholesterol sulfate accumulation in the stratum corneum. Distinctive features include large dark-brown scales that involve flexures and spare palms/soles—the opposite of ichthyosis vulgaris, which spares flexures and involves palms/soles. The 'dirty neck' appearance is characteristic of RXLI.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: In the X-LINKED CASTLE, a DIRTY SOOT-COVERED KNIGHT (dark brown scales) CRAWLS INTO THE FLEXURE DUNGEONS (scales encroach flexures) but REFUSES TO TOUCH THE SHINY GOLDEN PALMS AND SOLES (spares them completely)—the opposite of the clean-ELBOW ichthyosis vulgaris knight who hates dark basement creases.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with a rapidly enlarging, bright red pedunculated nodule on his finger that bleeds easily with minor trauma. Histology shows lobular proliferations of capillary endothelial cells within an oedematous stroma bounded by an epithelial collarette. According to ISSVA classification, how should this lesion be categorized?
opts: Benign vascular malformation
Benign vascular tumour
Congenital vascular anomaly
Granulomatous inflammatory disorder
questions.exp: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary haemangioma) is officially classified by ISSVA strictly under 'Benign Vascular Tumours,' deliberately separating it from vascular malformations. This reflects its acquired, clonal nature driven by somatic RAS/MAPK mutations rather than developmental vascular dysplasia.

questions.q: A 4-year-old girl presents with early-onset poikiloderma, hypoplastic thumbs, and absent radii. Genetic testing reveals compound heterozygous mutations in the RECQL4 gene. Which of the following malignancy risks is most significantly elevated in this patient?
opts: 32% risk of osteosarcoma
45% risk of lymphoma
No increased malignancy risk
25% risk of hepatocellular carcinoma
questions.exp: This clinical presentation—early-onset poikiloderma with severe skeletal abnormalities (radial ray defects, hypoplastic thumbs)—combined with RECQL4 mutations defines Rothmund-Thomson Syndrome Type II. Type II patients have a distinctive 32% risk of osteosarcoma, alongside increased cutaneous squamous and basal cell carcinoma risk. This profound malignancy predisposition is the absolute discriminating feature of Type II versus Type I.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a SKELETON made of BONE SARCOMAS (32% of them glowing red) dancing in the RADIAL castle tower at chromosome 8—the RECQL4 helicase guard collapses, unable to repair the DNA blueprint.

questions.q: Which of the following clinical features most reliably distinguishes livedo racemosa from physiological livedo reticularis?
opts: Symmetric pattern that completely resolves with warming in response to vasodilation
Asymmetric, irregular, broken pattern that persists despite warming and indicates underlying systemic disease
Localization exclusively to the distal lower extremities around the ankles
Presence of ulceration with scarring (atrophie blanche) in the perilesional skin
questions.exp: Livedo racemosa is distinctly asymmetric, irregular, branching, and 'broken' in appearance, typically more widespread, and characteristically does NOT completely resolve with warming—this persistence is a critical clinical marker for significant underlying systemic disease. In contrast, physiological livedo reticularis is benign, symmetric, uniform, and completely resolves upon warming, representing merely a transient vasospastic response.

questions.q: A 3-month-old boy presents with sparse, depigmented, lusterless hair that has a steel-wool texture. His skin is noted to be doughy, pale, and lax, particularly at the nape of the neck and axillae. He has developmental delay and seizures. Which gene mutation is responsible for this presentation?
opts: MITF gene on chromosome 3
ATP7A gene on chromosome Xq13.3
KIT gene on chromosome 4
SOX10 gene on chromosome 22
questions.exp: Menkes disease is caused by mutations in the ATP7A gene located on chromosome Xq13.3, which encodes a copper-transporting P-type ATPase. This defect prevents copper export from intestinal mucosa, leading to systemic copper deficiency and failure of copper-dependent enzymes including tyrosinase (causing depigmentation and abnormal hair) and cytochrome c oxidase (causing neurodegeneration). Classic presentation occurs at 2–3 months of age with the characteristic steel-wool hair and neurologic deterioration.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a COPPER PIPE (ATP7A) on the X-shaped chromosome staircase at Xq13.3, RUSTED and BROKEN—copper cannot flow out, so the castle's STEEL WOOL HAIR BRUSHES turn gray and the NEUROLOGIC TOWERS crumble.

questions.q: A 58-year-old man presents with sudden onset of ichthyosis-like scaling on his lower extremities that has progressively spread centrally over 3 months. He has no personal or family history of inherited skin disease. Physical examination reveals compact, plate-like scales with normal-appearing skin proximally. Which malignancy should be most actively investigated given the clinical presentation?
opts: Hodgkin Lymphoma
Breast carcinoma
Multiple Myeloma
Lung adenocarcinoma
questions.exp: Hodgkin Lymphoma is the single most common malignancy-associated acquired ichthyosis, occurring almost exclusively in adults with onset typically on lower extremities spreading centrally. The ichthyosis parallels disease activity and can precede, accompany, or follow lymphoma diagnosis.
questions.source: Acquired Ichthyosis (Paraneoplastic, Drug-Induced, Systemic Disease Associations — Hodgkin Lymphoma, HIV, Hypothyroidism, Sarcoidosis)

questions.q: A 6-year-old boy with Rothmund-Thomson syndrome develops bilateral cataracts requiring early surgical intervention. Genetic sequencing identifies mutations in the ANAPC1 gene located on chromosome 2q13. What is the expected malignancy risk profile in this patient?
opts: 32% lifetime risk of osteosarcoma
No increased incidence of malignancy
40% risk of cutaneous melanoma
60% risk of hematologic malignancies
questions.exp: ANAPC1 gene mutations define Rothmund-Thomson Syndrome Type I, which is distinguished clinically by the high incidence of juvenile cataracts (the original Rothmund presentation). Critically, Type I patients have NO increased incidence of malignancy—a cancer-sparing rule that contrasts sharply with the high malignancy burden in RECQL4-driven Type II disease.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: In the CATARACT CHAMBER on chromosome 2, the ANAPC1 guard stands SAFE behind a shield labeled 'NO CANCER'—while across the castle at chromosome 8, the RECQL4 tower BURNS with 32% osteosarcoma flames.

questions.q: A 2-year-old boy presents with fine, white-to-gray flaky scales on his extensor elbows and knees that spare the antecubital fossae. His mother reports the rash began at 4 months of age and worsens in winter. Skin examination reveals hyperlinear palms and soles. He has a history of mild asthma. Which genetic mutation is responsible for this presentation?
opts: Loss-of-function mutation in the FLG gene encoding filaggrin
Deletion of the STS gene encoding steroid sulfatase
Gain-of-function mutation in keratin-1 and keratin-10
Defect in gap junction protein connexin-43
questions.exp: Ichthyosis vulgaris is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the FLG gene on chromosome 1q21, which encodes filaggrin—a critical protein for keratin aggregation and stratum corneum hydration. The clinical presentation of fine scales on extensor surfaces sparing flexures, hyperlinear palms/soles, keratosis pilaris, and association with atopy (asthma) are pathognomonic for ichthyosis vulgaris.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture FILAGGRIN as a JANITOR in the stratum granulosum castle wing—when he's fired (loss-of-function), the WINTER HALLWAYS fill with FLAKY SNOW (fine scales) while the WARM SUMMER LIBRARY (humid summer) stays clean; the ATTIC ELBOWS (extensor surfaces) get dusty but the BASEMENT CREASES (flexures) mysteriously stay swept.

questions.q: An 11-year-old child of Indian descent presents with widespread erosive lichen planus with early onset and multiple relapses. Her father had a similar presentation in childhood. Which HLA allele is most strongly associated with familial childhood lichen planus with this erosive phenotype?
opts: HLA-A3
HLA-B27
HLA-B8
HLA-Bw35
questions.exp: Familial lichen planus in children is characterized by early onset, widespread erosive disease, and frequent relapses. HLA-B27, HLA-Aw19, HLA-B18, and HLA-Cw8 are specifically associated with familial cases, whereas HLA-A3, A5, A28, B8, B16, and Bw35 are associated with non-familial lichen planus.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: In the FAMILY VAULT, HLA-B27 guards stand with their EROSIVE SWORDS, protecting the inheritance of childhood LP; the other alleles guard only the scattered, sporadic courtyard.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with a permanent, asymmetric, branching violaceous mottling affecting her trunk and lower extremities that does not fully resolve with warming. Laboratory work reveals elevated anticardiolipin antibodies and a history of recurrent miscarriages. Which pathophysiologic mechanism best explains her cutaneous findings?
opts: Physiological vasospastic response to cold exposure affecting the superficial venous plexus
Intraluminal occlusion and thrombosis due to hypercoagulability pooling deoxygenated blood in predominantly venous areas
Non-inflammatory arteriolar obstruction causing segmental hyalinizing changes
Congenital developmental defect of the cutaneous microvasculature present at birth
questions.exp: Livedo racemosa is the asymmetric, permanent, branching form of livedo that serves as a hallmark cutaneous sign of antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APLS), occurring in up to 70% of SLE-associated APLS cases. The characteristic pattern results from intraluminal pathology causing thrombosis and occlusion, which impedes blood flow and causes pooling of deoxygenated blood in the superficial venous plexus at the margins of cutaneous vascular cones.

questions.q: A 52-year-old man presents with constitutional symptoms, abdominal pain, and peripheral neuropathy. Serological testing is negative for ANCA. Angiography reveals microaneurysms and stenoses at vessel bifurcations in mesenteric and renal arteries. Which vessel type is predominantly affected in this clinical presentation?
opts: Large elastic arteries
Medium-sized and small muscular arteries
Arterioles, capillaries, and venules
Small arteries with glomerular involvement
questions.exp: Polyarteritis nodosa is classified as a medium-vessel vasculitis that preferentially affects medium-sized and small muscular arteries, particularly at vessel bifurcations. The ANCA-negative status and absence of glomerulonephritis further confirm the diagnosis. Large vessel involvement and glomerulonephritis are not features of classic PAN.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture medium-SIZED KNIGHTS (medium vessels) clashing at the FORK IN THE ROAD (bifurcations) in the castle courtyard, while tiny ANCA spies are locked outside the gates.

questions.q: A 10-year-old child presents with pruritic, flat-topped purple papules on the flexural aspects of both wrists and ankles. The lesions exhibit new linear eruptions along scratch marks from trauma. Which of the following best describes the primary immunopathological mechanism driving this condition?
opts: IgG and IgA autoantibodies against basal keratinocytes detected on direct immunofluorescence
CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocytes recruited by CXCR-3+ NK cells attacking basal keratinocytes at the dermo-epidermal junction
Circulating immune complex deposition along the basement membrane zone
Th2-mediated humoral response with eosinophilic infiltration
questions.exp: Lichen planus is a T-cell-mediated autoimmune disorder, not an antibody-driven disease. CD56+ CD16- NK cells expressing CXCR-3 secrete IFN-γ and TNF-α, recruiting CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocytes that directly target basal keratinocytes at the DEJ. Direct immunofluorescence is negative or shows only non-specific secondary phenomena like fibrinogen deposition.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine EIGHT (CD8) WARRIORS in armored suits storming the BASEMENT (basal layer) of the castle keep, summoned by CXCR-3 trumpet blasts from the NK knights above—no IgG guards needed.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with erythema nodosum characterized by painful subcutaneous nodules on the shins. Initial investigations exclude systemic causes including tuberculosis and sarcoidosis. Which of the following NSAIDs and dosing regimens is considered first-line therapy for symptomatic management of uncomplicated erythema nodosum?
opts: Ibuprofen 200 mg twice daily
Naproxen 250–500 mg twice daily or 500 mg daily
Indomethacin 10–15 mg daily as initial monotherapy
Aspirin 75 mg daily for antiplatelet effect
questions.exp: Naproxen at 250–500 mg twice daily or 500 mg daily is highlighted as a highly efficacious and frequently recommended primary NSAID option for first-line symptomatic management of erythema nodosum. NSAIDs are the gold standard for pain relief and accelerating resolution of inflammatory lesions in uncomplicated, non-debilitating EN.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman with darker skin phototype presents with slate-gray discoloration over areas of previous severe inflammatory acne. Under Wood's lamp examination, the pigment appears blurry and does not accentuate. Histologically, vacuolar degeneration of basal keratinocytes with melanin-laden macrophages in the superficial dermis is noted. Which type of PIH does this clinical and histopathological presentation represent?
opts: Epidermal PIH with increased melanocyte number
Dermal PIH with pigment incontinence
Mixed PIH with equal epidermal and dermal involvement
Epidermal PIH with accelerated melanosome transfer
questions.exp: The slate-gray coloration due to the Tyndall effect, blurry appearance on Wood's lamp (non-accentuating), and histological finding of melanophages in the superficial dermis with vacuolar damage to basal keratinocytes are pathognomonic for dermal PIH. Dermal PIH results from pigment incontinence—the release of free melanin into the dermis—and is notoriously refractory to treatment.

questions.q: A 10-month-old with severe, untreated diaper dermatitis develops multiple 1–2 cm reddish-purplish nodules over the convex areas of the diaper region. Histopathology reveals a dense mixed dermal infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils, and eosinophils, but no true granulomas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sarcoidosis with diaper distribution
Granuloma gluteale infantum (infantile gluteal granuloma)
Tuberculoid leprosy presenting in infancy
Crohn's disease with cutaneous involvement
questions.exp: Granuloma gluteale infantum is a severe, hyperplastic tissue reaction to chronic irritation, Candida infection, or potent corticosteroid use in the diaper area, presenting as violaceous nodules (0.5–3 cm) over convex surfaces. Despite its misleading name, histology shows no true granulomas—only dense mixed dermal inflammation with lymphocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils, and eosinophils, distinguishing it from genuine granulomatous conditions.

questions.q: A 28-year-old patient requires anesthesia for a laceration repair on the index finger. Using the dorsal approach for digital nerve block, what is the maximum recommended volume of local anesthetic per side to prevent ischemic compression injury?
opts: Less than 0.5 mL per side
Less than 1.5 mL per side
Less than 2.5 mL per side
Less than 3.5 mL per side
questions.exp: The dorsal approach (proximal digital block) requires strict volume limitation to <1.5 mL per side to prevent tourniquet/tamponade effects from excessive fluid compression causing mechanical ischemia. Total volume across both sides should therefore not exceed 3 mL. Historical ischemic complications were caused by excessive volumes, not by epinephrine as previously believed.

questions.q: A clinician performs a posterior tibial nerve block for sole anesthesia. The needle is inserted at a 45° angle just posterior to the palpated tibial artery pulse and contacts bone. What is the appropriate next step?
opts: Advance the needle 2–3 mm further into the bone to ensure maximum anesthetic spread
Withdraw the needle slightly to avoid periosteal injection and deposit 3–7 mL of local anesthetic
Immediately redirect the needle at a 90° angle and re-advance
Withdraw completely and attempt the block at a different anatomical site
questions.exp: Once bone contact is achieved during posterior tibial nerve block, the needle must be withdrawn slightly to avoid periosteal injection, which is painful and unnecessary. The local anesthetic (3–7 mL) is then deposited at this withdrawn position to block the posterior tibial nerve in the tarsal tunnel region. This technique safely blocks the nerve before it divides into medial and lateral plantar branches.

questions.q: A 7-year-old child presents with tender suboccipital and postauricular lymphadenopathy followed 5 days later by a discrete, light pink maculopapular rash on the face that spreads caudally. The rash fades within 3 days. Which virus is most likely responsible?
opts: Measles virus (Paramyxoviridae)
Rubella virus (Togaviridae)
Varicella-zoster virus (Herpesviridae)
Parvovirus B19 (Parvoviridae)
questions.exp: Rubella characteristically presents with prodromal lymphadenopathy (suboccipital, postauricular, cervical) that precedes the rash by up to 7 days, followed by a discrete, fainter, non-coalescing maculopapular exanthem that fades rapidly (within 3 days). The rash is notably fainter and less confluent than measles. The virus belongs to the genus Rubivirus within the Togaviridae family.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a RUBELLA RUBY GEM in the CASTLE EARS & NECK CORRIDOR (lymphadenopathy location) arriving 7 days BEFORE a faint PINK BALL gown (discrete, light pink rash) sweeps down the grand staircase in just 3 days.

questions.q: A 17-year-old girl with confirmed EBV-positive infectious mononucleosis develops an intensely confluent, bright red, pruritic maculopapular rash 8 days after starting ampicillin for presumed streptococcal pharyngitis. You counsel the patient regarding future antibiotic use. Which statement is most accurate regarding this ampicillin rash?
opts: This represents a true penicillin allergy and all β-lactams must be permanently avoided
This is NOT a true penicillin allergy but rather a transient EBV-induced immunological cross-reaction; penicillins can be safely used in future infections
The rash is caused by direct toxic effects of ampicillin on EBV-infected epithelial cells and will recur with any aminopenicillin
This indicates genetic predisposition to β-lactam hypersensitivity and alternative antibiotics should be used exclusively
questions.exp: The ampicillin rash in IM occurs through EBV-induced polyclonal B-cell activation producing IgM antibodies against aminopenicillins, forming immune complexes—NOT a true allergic reaction. This transient virus-driven immunological cross-reaction does not preclude future safe use of penicillins once acute EBV infection resolves. Modern incidence is ~30%, historically up to 90–100%, and the rash typically resolves within one week despite continued ampicillin therapy.
questions.source: EBV Cutaneous Manifestations (Infectious Mononucleosis, Ampicillin Rash, Gianotti-Crosti)
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Imagine EBV as a ROGUE PUPPETEER making B-cells dance and throw AMPICILLIN-SHAPED DARTS at innocent skin—it's a TEMPORARY BETRAYAL, not a lifetime feud. Once the puppeteer leaves, the B-cells forgive penicillin again.

questions.q: Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) is detected in a patient with newly diagnosed polyarteritis nodosa. Which immunopathological mechanism explains HBV-associated PAN?
opts: Direct viral invasion of arterial endothelial cells with lytic destruction
Formation and deposition of immune complexes containing HBsAg and immunoglobulins
ANCA-mediated activation of neutrophils at the vessel wall
T-cell mediated granulomatous inflammation of medium vessels
questions.exp: HBV-associated PAN is driven by immune complex-mediated vascular damage, where complexes containing hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and corresponding immunoglobulins deposit in medium-vessel walls, triggering necrotizing inflammation. This mechanism explains why up to 30% of classic PAN cases were historically associated with active HBV infection before widespread HBV vaccination.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine HBsAg (little SPIKY BALLS) and antibodies (STICKY GLUE) forming IMMUNE COMPLEX CEMENT that hardens on the castle walls, cracking and crumbling the MEDIUM-SIZED STONE ARCHES (medium vessels).

questions.q: A 42-year-old man with known HIV infection presents with severe generalized xerosis and massive plate-like scales beginning on his lower legs. Laboratory studies reveal a CD4 count of 35 cells/mm³. What is the pathophysiologic basis for acquired ichthyosis development in this patient?
opts: Direct viral invasion of keratinocytes causing cytolysis
Massive CD4+ T-cell depletion disrupting keratinocyte homeostasis and cornification
Opportunistic fungal infection of the stratum corneum
Secondary hypothyroidism from chronic HIV-related inflammation
questions.exp: In HIV/AIDS, acquired ichthyosis develops only after profound CD4+ T-cell depletion (typically <50 cells/mm³) and serves as a clinical marker for severe immunosuppression. Loss of CD4+ T-cell-mediated immune surveillance directly disrupts normal keratinocyte differentiation and cornification.
questions.source: Acquired Ichthyosis (Paraneoplastic, Drug-Induced, Systemic Disease Associations — Hodgkin Lymphoma, HIV, Hypothyroidism, Sarcoidosis)

questions.q: Which of the following inflammatory mediators and their mechanism BEST explains the pathogenesis of postinflammatory hyperpigmentation?
opts: Autoantibodies targeting melanocyte-specific antigens, similar to vitiligo pathogenesis
Arachidonic acid metabolites and cytokines (IL-1, TNF-α, PGE2) binding to melanocyte receptors to upregulate tyrosinase activity
Permanent reduction in melanocyte number due to inflammatory destruction
Selective proliferation of melanocytes driven by growth hormone signaling
questions.exp: PIH is fundamentally a physiologic reactive response, not an autoimmune condition. Inflammatory mediators including leukotrienes, prostaglandins (PGE2, PGD2), IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, and ROS bind to melanocyte surface receptors, upregulating tyrosinase and melanosome synthesis and transfer. Unlike vitiligo or pemphigus, there is no target autoantigen involved.

questions.q: A 28-year-old pregnant woman in her second trimester develops a bleeding nodule on the anterior maxillary gingiva. She is concerned about malignancy. Which statement most accurately reflects the true nature and prognosis of this lesion?
opts: It is a true granuloma caused by pyogenic bacteria requiring oral antibiotics
It is a reactive vascular hyperplasia that may spontaneously regress postpartum despite its rapid growth
It is a malignant vascular tumour with high risk of metastasis and requires urgent chemotherapy
It is a permanent congenital vascular malformation that will enlarge throughout pregnancy
questions.exp: The historical name 'pyogenic granuloma' is a double misnomer—it is neither pyogenic (not bacterial) nor a true granuloma (lacks multinucleated giant cells and epithelioid histiocytes). In pregnancy ('granuloma gravidarum'), these reactive vascular hyperplasias often undergo partial or complete spontaneous regression in the postpartum period despite rapid growth during pregnancy.

questions.q: Regarding the use of epinephrine in digital nerve blocks, which statement reflects current evidence-based practice?
opts: Epinephrine is absolutely contraindicated in all digital blocks due to irreversible ischemic necrosis
Commercial lidocaine with epinephrine (1:100,000–1:200,000) is exceptionally safe for digital blocks, and historical ischemic events were caused by mechanical tamponade or non-commercial mixtures
Epinephrine should only be used in fingers but never in toes
Epinephrine-containing solutions require special preparation and have higher risk than plain lidocaine
questions.exp: Modern multicenter studies have definitively disproven the historical myth that epinephrine causes ischemic necrosis in digital blocks. Commercial lidocaine with epinephrine at standard concentrations (1:100,000 or 1:200,000) is proven safe; historical complications resulted from excessive volume (mechanical compression), non-commercial preparations, or older vasoconstrictors like cocaine. However, cautious avoidance remains acceptable in patients with severe peripheral vascular disease, diabetes, or Raynaud's phenomenon.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man with a 5-year history of Crohn's disease now develops erythema nodosum. His gastroenterologist requests a dermatology consultation regarding NSAID use for pain control. What is the appropriate recommendation?
opts: NSAIDs are safe and should be initiated at standard doses for EN symptom control
NSAIDs are absolutely contraindicated or must be used with extreme caution due to the significant risk of provoking a severe exacerbation of underlying bowel inflammation
Low-dose aspirin monotherapy is preferred as it has no gastrointestinal effects
Indomethacin should be used instead as it has superior bowel safety compared to other NSAIDs
questions.exp: NSAIDs are absolutely contraindicated or must be used with extreme caution in patients whose erythema nodosum is a reactive manifestation of underlying inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), including Crohn's disease, due to the significant risk of provoking severe exacerbation of the underlying bowel inflammation. This is a crucial contraindication that requires careful patient screening before NSAID initiation.

questions.q: A 9-month-old infant presents with erythematous, glazed dermatitis on the buttocks, lower abdomen, and medial thighs, with characteristic sparing of the deep inguinal folds and gluteal cleft. Which of the following best explains the preserved skin in the spared areas?
opts: Enhanced sebaceous gland activity in the intertriginous regions
Lower occlusion, moisture, and friction in the deep skin folds compared to convex surfaces
Autoimmune tolerance specific to the gluteal cleft mediated by regulatory T cells
Presence of protective Candida colonization in the inguinal folds
questions.exp: Primary irritant diaper dermatitis affects convex surfaces (buttocks, lower abdomen, medial thighs) in direct contact with the diaper, while sparing the deep inguinal folds and gluteal cleft. This distribution pattern reflects differential exposure to urine, feces, friction, and occlusion—the deep folds experience less direct contact and friction, hence preservation. The condition is purely irritant-driven, not autoimmune.
